blocks.x: I'd like to get your real name down first.

My name is John Eblen, E-B-L-E-N, Rau, R-A-U. And the John Eblen comes from my grandfather, who lived, he had the whole square on Arabella, Nashville, Hurst, and Garfield. He owned that whole square, and he bought it for about $1,500 when he came over here from Germany.
Could I run it by? It looks like the real's walked, I thought.
Rick, I'll put you in charge of seeing if it picks our voices up.
Okay? All right. Yeah. You think the microphone's gone bad? It's hardly picking my voice up at all.

I'll speak up, though. So you're of German descent? Right. I'm one of the few pure Germans you know. My grandfather and grandmothers on both sides were born in Germany. One of them, the Eblens came from Stuttgart. And Rau, my father's family, came from Bremen. So they were both born in this country. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. !
It's rolling now, the second reel of that Monroe. Go ahead, you want to ask them first.
I was wondering about the nature of that particular occasion of that photograph at the Chess Checkers.

Well, it was an old script dance. I don't know who promoted it. We used to have two or three people that made a living out of it, that kept themselves in school by giving these script dances every once in a while. Most of them were given a two-lane gym, the old gym. But this happened to be one given down what was then the Cosmopolitan Hotel, and it went all the way through from Bourbon to Royal Street. It went completely through the block. But the part on Bourbon Street was called the Chess and Checkers Club. They rented it, and they used to lease it out for income to individuals and organizations. And this particular occasion happened to be a script dance that somebody gave, whom I don't remember at the particular time. But that's the one you see with Dick and all of us in there. I'm sitting in the back, standing in the back, holding a fiddle in my hand that looks like a bunch of flowers. I could never make it out.
You wouldn't know that I was a fiddle.

I didn't open the fiddle on you. It should have been a fiddle. But the other one, I mean, the one that was taken in the Blue Room, was more or less a regular musician picture. I mean, we were all apparently playing. It was a formal picture.
And I was wondering about the attire that you were wearing at the Chess and Checkers Club. It was very casual.
Well, it was a Bowery party. That's what they called it.
So it was a special occasion, a special theme of some kind.

Yeah. They gave it a name, and everybody was dressed up in raggedy clothes, anything they could think of. You know, for the, I don't know, I think it was a stick, I mean, a red hat on a big derby, if I'm not mistaken. And a cigar on his mouth.
Yeah. And Benji White had a black eye, it looks like. That's right. Yeah.
Did you ever see that? Yeah. That's funny. And Monk Smith had a stupid look in his face. He was on the front row.
And my dad had his eyes closed for some reason. He was only a real kid then, and I think he must have been 16 years old.

Yeah, I think Dick had just started playing with us then. He didn't come into the picture until a few years after we got started. But up until that time we were more or less a string band. We didn't have a couple of saxophone players. That was Benji White and Monk Smith.
Well he was originally a guitarist with the string group, wasn't he?

Yeah. It was Monk played the guitar. I remember he had a hell of a fine guitar. Somebody had bought over in Italy and brought to this country. I think it was Bill Kleppinger. He was one of his good friends. I think Bill lived at his house. He was living on Napoleon and Ronaldette I believe it was. We had quite a vogue at one time. I don't know how it got started, but a few years in there we played for practically all the fraternity parties around Tulane and most of the balls. The carnival season was just getting reorganized after the war. We got in on the ground floor, out through Earl Crum. He was a promoter. He had all the contacts. They used to call him Sleepy. He looked like he was sleeping all the time while he was playing the drums. I think half the time he was. He was a good promoter. Maybe it was better that he was asleep. But he did. I mean his mother ran that shop on Lee Circle there. She also had a few boarders. Her little house is still there. I think it's some kind of a cocktail lounge or something right as you turn the corner.
On the uptown riverside there? Yeah. Another one near the environment. A little Victorian. That's a nice house.

We used to, all the kings, all the parades used to stop there and have champagne when they were living in Africa. And we'd be up there playing music for our own benefit half the time. We did a lot of our practicing in that little house. So I got to know it real well.
Well, was that at the time the olives were still largely a string group or was that after the transition to the winds?

Well, it was between times. I mean we started off as a string group in there. I think they used to call it the Invincibles, I believe was one of their names. But we had a little outfit that started over on the Gulf Coast. I remember I had to quit school. I mean I'd started to work and they made this arrangement over there at the Miramar Hotel. They played part of the time at the Miramar Hotel, which is where the big hotel is, the one that just blew up a few years ago. We'd go on a streetcar that used to run right along the beach. We'd spend two days and nights down there and two days and nights down at the Miramar and we'd play it Saturday night at the Miramar. And that was mostly string band stuff. And then we'd come to town on a, what would you call it? Anyway, we'd go out to Pierron's and play the music at it, Spanish Fort, Pierron's band. Oh yeah. That was our picnic. We'd come to listen to music on a Monday night. We'd have off.
Did you ever go to Trancinas?

Well, this was what they used to call Trancinas in those days. It was at Spanish Fort and Pierron's band was the one that was famous there for many years. We'd go out there, we'd take a streetcar, I remember in those days. You'd get on a streetcar at Canal Street and go all the way out to Spanish Fort. That band used to be playing out there in those days.
Was that band playing what you would call jazz as opposed to what you used to hear and you used to hear?

It was New Orleans jazz, but it wasn't loud music. Pierron was a violinist and he had guitar playing, they had Sweet Ammo playing the piano and two or three others in there. I don't think they had any brass instruments in there. They probably had a couple of saxophones or something like that. But it was pretty music. I mean, he was well known. They had wonderful timing. Everybody used to love to go out there to dance. And when they went out there, they danced. It was just a place that people would go to. It had a vogue for a few years. And that was the place to go. Later on, it was the West End Roof. That was when your father and Red and that bunch, I quit by then. Yeah, that's right.
Dad played out the West End Roof for a while, but it wasn't much longer than that he quit.

I don't think he played out there very long, no. I remember going out there on two or three occasions and sitting with them. But I never played much at that time. Most of my recollection of the West End Roof was coming in on a sailboat. They would, all the people would watch us coming in there. Because it made so damn much noise. Did you ever go to Agnes Boathouse out there? I had a friend who had a boat called Backe. He had a schooner. He had a two-cylinder engine that made enough noise you could hear it across Mandeville. All the people on the West End Roof would quit dancing to come watch us come in there because it made so damn much noise.
Did you ever go to Agnes Boathouse out there?

Hell yes. Agnes Boathouse was a monk and Rene Jelper. I used to play way back in the olden days. I know Daddy Knight was still living. Daddy Knight and Johnny Luther and one other person had the Boathouse there. We used to spend most weekends out there during the summertime. We'd go somewhere and end up either in the Agnes Boathouse or the one next door to it that Bill Edgar had. It was, remember old Fats, what's his name? Fats Daly, you remember him? I heard of him. He wasn't a musician but he was one of our favorite drinkers. Great fan of your music. He used to make an oar hen at the Agnes Boathouse and a barrel and that stud was an oar. They'd make it by the gallon. It was quite potent I might add too.
There was a place out there to sleep, wasn't there? Yeah. You'd learn to play music late and stay over.

They had half a dozen punks between the two boathouses there in several places. Later on I had a boathouse further out the wharf there where I used to keep my boat. I had the SIS at that time. We had a boathouse we built together with Leslie Deird and Ben Ravenach. They had half of it. Wallace Petar and I had the other half. They had the one boat. I had the other one right next to each other. So it was quite a famous and infamous place.
I hate to keep skipping around but I get confused on some of these people that you played with. Did you ever know Guy Lahneman? I knew Guy very well, yeah. Who was he?

He played an instrument that he made out of a shoebox and a car horn. And he could play the damn thing like nobody's business. And he would sing too. I mean he had a sort of a voice like Edmond Sushant. It was one of these grating sort of thing. But he knew how to put it over. They had a wonderful sense of rhythm. And that was Guy's instrument. They had a wooden box about that big with a shoehorn. Not a shoehorn. A car bell nailed onto the damn thing. Between the wooden box and the car bell that was Guy made his music. And he was damn good at it too. Guy was one of the, we called ourselves the college quintet when we were playing over on the Gulf Coast. And that came back to town and evolved into different outfits. And that's about the time I got out of it. Because they started playing professionally. I don't think Guy ever played. He was a pretty damn good life insurance man. He was one of the best in town as a matter of fact, as a young man. But some of the boys got mixed up in the thing professionally and they were playing music. And I had this job here. I mean, I was, this was my father's business. And he got tired of me monkeying around. So I got down here in the tobacco business. But that goes back, as I said before, to W.R.A.B., who was in the tobacco business. And this outfit was in trouble financially. An old man, Duke, the original James P. Duke of the tobacco company, American Tobacco Company, sent down to Mr. Irby to see if he couldn't find somebody to take this thing over. So Mr. Irby talked to my father. And my father said, well, he'd give it a try if he could get somebody to handle the sales of him, because he wasn't a salesman. So that's where the DeBens came into the picture. The Chairs DeBens was the father of these boys here. And grandfathers, some of them. And between them, they raised enough money. Mr. DeBens, my father, and his brother raised enough money to float this, get it started. And that was the beginning of the, I think they raised $20,000 between them. And assumed the debts, of course, which it was. But they were then still part of the American Tobacco Company. They hadn't paid up everything yet at that time. And they used to, the American Tobacco Company, put in their bookkeeping system, accounting system. And my father was always very proud of it, because he thought it was way ahead of its time for concern our size. But we used to, I remember his, having to send reports up to New York every month. And, up until the time they paid out their debt, we were still, ostensibly, part of the American Tobacco Company. And, up until the time they got started. It took a little while to get it straightened out, but they did. And that, that's how I happened to be in there, because he was my father and my father was Mr. Irby's secretary. Mr. Irby was the Irby branch of the League of Mine Tobacco Company. So, I'd add it up to the tobacco business instead of me being a musician or a schoolteacher. I would have liked to teach at Tulane. I liked teaching, but there wasn't much money in it, as you can see. I got paid $850 for the whole year.
What about Eugene Jinx Dybal? Did you know him? I may not be pronouncing that name right.

Dybal, yeah, that's right. He was with us way back there, and so long ago I can't remember him too well. What did he play? He wasn't playing any music as far as I remember. I'm talking about we had a Dybal that worked for us in this company. I think he was in the stock department.
You may be talking about somebody else. This is at the Miramar, I think. I think Benji White told me about him. Well? Fred Ogden? Fred Ogden.

It was Fred Ogden, Benji White, Monk Smith. Oh, not Dybal, I know who you're talking about. Debal. Debal. Debal. He was the architect. He was the architect. He was the worst musician we had. He didn't claim to be much of a musician, but Fritz Ogden used to tell him, remember, six, five, three, and he would change his chord when he was playing on the thing. That's the only reason he knew how to change it. They had him fixed up that way. But he got along all right. But that was Jinx.
Fred Ogden is Fritz Ogden?

Yeah, Fred Ogden is Fritz. He committed suicide a few years ago, remember? No. Yeah, he lived right around the corner from where I was living at that time on, what the hell street was it? Thad and Chestnut, I believe. He walked right down there, half a block down, right the same street where he lived and shot himself right out on the street. That was Fritz, or Fred as we called him. Fred got to be quite a big shot, not a big shot, but I mean he had a very profitable investment business. That was his business. He was mixed up with one of these outfit stock and bond deals. That was his. And I think the thing that made him commit suicide was not any financial trouble, but he had a kind of cancer situation.
Oh yeah.
And it must have become pretty painful for him. Apparently there was no way out of it. I mean, he was just questioning how long he was going to last, so he took that way out of
it. Oh, a messy way.
Benji, still in the round. I see him every once in a while.
I like his phone number. He moved. I never see him anymore.
I see.
Well, he ought to be in here. He was out on Maryland, wasn't he?
I think he was, yeah.

And then he, I have been trying to find him. He was working down at what? Swigman's, you know, they closed down the late brothers on Canal Street. So they all moved away. And I had an awful time finding him. I didn't check some things out.
I saw Benji out at the Yacht Club not too long ago. There's a Benjamin J. White at Lamarck. I don't even know where that is.
That's in Algiers. Huh? That's in Algiers.

Well, maybe it is in Algiers. I think that was his… It's the only Benji in here. Benjamin… It's not Benji J., it's Benjamin. They've got it. B-E-N-J in there. 1115 Lamarck. That's the only one in there. Well, I'll have to check it again because it's been, you know, several years since I've tried to call him. I just wanted to talk to him about things. I found a lot of notes I had on the Owl. And I wanted to tell you about that too today. I've been going through my old notes that I made with Johnny Harmon years ago and I've

been going through my old notes that I've been going through my old notes that I've made with Johnny Harmon years ago and… I must have gotten a lot of information from Pinky one time, and Benji. Because there was such a change over in the band. Pinky came in after I left.
I mean, I knew Pinky very well. As a matter of fact, they used to have dates with my present wife way back then. I was not playing the band at the same time Pinky was.
Oh what did Fred Ogden play? I forgot to ask that.
Fred played the banjo if I'm not mistaken.
And he had a good ear for changes? Yeah, he had a good ear.

But he also had a nice sense of humor. He could tell these funny stories that went along with our type of entertainment there. But if I'm not mistaken, Fritz at that time was playing the banjo or some kind of makeshift banjo, banjo mandolin or something, I don't know what the hell they called it. I don't think it was a straight banjo. That was the little Frenchman played the banjo. Oh, I know who you're talking about. Five string, a four string, a six string? I think he had a six string. He could play a damn thing like nobody's business. He could play tunes on it and everything else.
Was this before Rene Jelpie or after him?
This was Rene Jelpie.
Oh, I see.

I'm trying to talk about it now, yeah. I didn't want to put words in your mouth. No, this was Rene. He and I and Monk used to play as strings sometimes. There'd be various people who'd mix in there sometime along the line.

But I was out of the band when Pinky came along. It's hard for me to get the picture of this band at the Miramar in my mind now, today, how they would have sounded with all those different instruments. Now, who carried the lead? I did. You did. Did you play a straight lead or would you call it a hot lead? Swinging, variations?

I suppose we'd vary it. I mean, part of the time would be just straight music and then part of the time would put some kind of variations on it. I started trying to imitate one of the woodwinds or something like that. I mean, it was a strange band, I can tell you that. This outfit we had there, we were playing for the guests at the hotel. Sometimes I was still a fairly proficient violinist at that time. And I could play solos for a half hour at a time without repeating the same thing, because I had a pretty good background in straight music at that time. The jazz part of it came in just by accident, I mean just by my friends.
Did you know harmony? No. You hadn't studied a chord, actually? No.

No. I wasn't any good at that. But all I was good for was I was the only one in the band who could read music. So if they got a new tune sometime on sheet music or something I could dig out the main line and they would work from there on. But what did Benji play like? Benji was pretty damn good. He learned the saxophone over our dead bodies when we were living over at Miramar. They had an old cottage that turned over to us. And while we were taking our afternoon nap, Benji was working on the goddamn saxophone, keeping us all awake.
But what kind of part did he play? Would he play a second part or would it be a variation, a counter melody, an oblicato? Could you remember?
I think Benji played more or less the lead. I mean the straight part of it and then he would improvise on it too.
Did you all work out duets where you played variations together?

Yeah, we had little things that sort of worked themselves out over a period of time. No matter how they happened, they just worked themselves out. But I was not capable of making chords or anything like that. All I could do was play the lead.

But some people played, you know, they run the chords up and down on the instrument and stuff like that. They know the chords. And then other people played variations on the melody and just different approaches to playing.

Well, I would say that Benji, he started off playing the violin with us. And then he got into this saxophone. And then on, he and Monk were the two saxophonists. And I really don't know who played which. I mean it was all mixed up together. I think Monk was more or less the background man. I think Benji was the lead. He'd put in the variations or whatever he could think of.

As I remember it from what Benji told me, Benji played alto and Monk played tenor. Some Monk would harmonize with him. Yeah. But at one time they were playing C melody too, both of them. And I think in that picture they were on C melody, but I'm not sure. Because you know the C melody was so popular. Of course you could read piano copies of the C melody sax. You wouldn't have to transpose or anything. That made it very handy for a little light band. Well, I think that's what we tried to do.

That's the only thing we could do as a matter of fact, too. We got this out of tune piano and that's why. We couldn't, it was so far out of tune that we couldn't get the instruments tuned back in there and that's when some of these bars were pretty damn good at it and started transposing and we finally ended up being able to play on this out of tune piano. It wasn't necessarily out of tune, it was out of pitch. I mean it was about a half note, three quarters of a note off of what it was supposed to be. And when you tried to tune the saxophones into that and the trumpet just didn't work.
How long had my uncle played with the band at that time?

Oh, I would say three or four years. I mean he played, he was still playing when I wasn't anymore, I know that. I think he was still playing when Pinky was in there with him if I'm not mistaken. Pinky Vodakovic.
I'm not sure. I thought that about that time he had left the band.
Well maybe he did. I don't know. I mean because we'd both.

LeBlanc had come in there at one point. Now wait a minute. Who was playing bass? LeBlanc? Dan LeBlanc? LeBlanc was playing trombone? No, Red played the bass the only time we had one. But later on, Netto and LeBlanc came in there. I can't remember which played bass and which played trombone. It must have been Frank Netto on trombone and Dan LeBlanc on bass.
Frank Netto played bass. As a matter of fact, we had his bass in the middle of the house for years.
Well I think they both doubled and so I get confused. You know it's hard to remember everything like that.
Well all I remember was Red had the hell of a time getting that instrument around there sometimes and they were strapped on top of the car with the rain falling down the hole.
I remember when Rene Jalpe played, how did he work it? Did he strum chords or did he pick with his fingers?
Do you remember? He picked with his fingers.
So he would be playing something that was pretty complex.

He would be playing the melody and variations on the melody and everything else. He played it like nobody ever heard before. I agree. And he taught himself. I mean I don't think he ever had a lesson in his life. But he picked it up somewhere along the line and he played it extremely well.
And Monk Smith, did he play fingerstyle or strumming?
When he played he was strumming. He had a great big old guitar and he was just playing chords strumming.

That works out very well with the lower register clarinet that Pinky used to play on the records. You have to hear all those records. Those records are still great. When they go back to the two string instruments you can get some feeling of what the Invincibles and the old 6 and 7 8s must have sounded like. But they'd never been a violin on those records.

No, I remember the first time I went to the 6 and 7 8s was playing at a two lane night. And they had two violins in it at that time. And this was playing on the old two lane stage if I'm not mistaken. I'm trying to think. Midget Harrison, who people used to confuse with me and Vice Facer all the time because both little runts we both played the violin was one of them and Rex Rajak was the other violin. And this was in a, what they then called the 6 and 7 8s. I think Midget was the 7 8s. The origin of the name. The origin of the name. The big guy. One more again.

You were with the, oh go ahead. We can stop this. We can stop this. Okay. If you want to make a phone call or something, the tape is just about to run out now. Oh no, that's all right. We can stop for a minute. No, this, I know who this is.
This is somebody I've been trying to get in touch with for a meeting. Didn't have to be a big. Oh, I see. I'll call him later.
Well, what about the, uh, Paché Club? I wanted to...

This is one of our early deals at what we called a quartier club in that days. And it was a script dance of some sorts. I don't know who gave it. But I remember one poor guy was dressed up as a, what would you call it? He just had a loin cloth on and some kind of skin over his shoulder and it was cold as hell. And we found him and passed out in the back of the yard. How the hell did he get pneumonia? I don't know, maybe he did, but we never heard from him further. We got him in there. And that was when Red was playing the piano. And I was playing the violin. The air crumb was playing. And we ended up, just about three of us, playing the rest of the band.
